messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Security Guard
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 71-year-old married American man who has worked for years as a security guard, and when he describes the day that split his life into before and after, he does so in fragments that are strangely exact. He had been on duty when the terrorist attack happened, in a public building where part of his job was to watch entrances, notice unusual movement, and be the person others depended on if something went wrong. He remembers particular visual details with painful precision: the angle of a doorway, the sudden movement of people turning all at once, the look of panic spreading faster than he could process it. Certain moments remain so clear and sharply outlined that they seem more like scenes he is still inside than events that are over. Yet when he tries to put the whole thing into order from beginning to end, he loses the thread. He can tell one vivid piece, then another, but not a full coherent account that makes sense to him. At times he recounts it with no feeling at all, sounding almost puzzled by his own flatness, as if he is describing something that happened to another guard in another city.

What has stayed with David most strongly is the sense that he was in the role he was supposed to fulfill and still could not stop what happened. He had gone into that line of work with a clear idea of himself as someone who protected people, someone steady in danger, someone who would know what to do. In the aftermath, he had come to believe that he had failed in the most important role in his life. Even now he compares himself harshly to an imagined other man, certain that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, or would have seen more, reacted faster, done something decisive before the attack unfolded. When he says this, it is not boastful fantasy turned inward but a settled conviction. He speaks as if the event exposed something weak and inadequate in him.

Over the months that followed, David found himself scanning people almost automatically, especially men whose movements seemed abrupt, whose clothes looked bulky, or who appeared to be watching others too closely. In his job as a security guard, this constant vigilance blends uneasily with what is expected of him. He is already supposed to observe, but he notices that his attention no longer feels measured or professional. At work he tracks faces, hands, exits, and body positions in a way that leaves him exhausted by the end of a shift. In break rooms, diners, even family restaurants, he always chooses the seat with his back to the wall so he can see the door and the whole room. If that seat is taken, he becomes tense and distracted, sometimes insisting on moving or waiting for another table. To him this is simple common sense; being unable to see who is coming feels like handing himself over blindly.

His mind also circles repeatedly around revenge. He spends long stretches thinking about how he would get even with the assailant, replaying possibilities in detail, imagining confrontation, imagining justice that feels personal rather than abstract. He recognizes that these thoughts do not lead anywhere practical, especially because the attack is over and the fantasy cannot alter what happened, but he returns to them anyway. The ruminations seem to grip him most when he is alone after work or awake in the early morning beside his wife, staring into the dark.

David describes himself now as unable to deal with even the slightest upset. A scheduling change at work, a minor disagreement at home, an unexpected noise in a store can leave him feeling overwhelmed in a way he finds humiliating. This frightens him almost as much as the memories themselves. He had always thought of himself as steady, and now small disruptions feel like proof that something essential in him has given way. His wife has seen him become more rigid about where he sits and more preoccupied with watching strangers, and although he remains employed, the habits have narrowed his world. Meals out are planned around where he can position himself. Ordinary errands take longer because he keeps assessing the people around him.

By the time he comes for help, David is tired of living as if every room needs to be secured before he can breathe. He is also tired of not being able to tell a clear story about the attack despite remembering parts of it in such piercing detail. What finally brings him in is the sense that his life has become organized around danger and self-reproach. He wants, cautiously, to feel like himself again with his wife and at work. What he fears most is that the attack revealed a permanent truth—that he failed when it mattered, and that he no longer has the capacity to handle even ordinary life.
